opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, less than people might expect, though it's a different kind of bureaucracy.

People assume government means endless paperwork, and some of that is real. There are procurement rules, security processes, and a lot of thought about how money gets spent, because it's public money and there's accountability attached. Hiring especially can be slower than in industry. We've worked hard to make it faster, but there are constraints you just don't have at a company.

But DeepMind isn't bureaucracy-free either. It's part of Google, which is a very large organization with its own processes, approvals, and layers. When you want to publish something, start a project, or get compute, there are steps to go through. They're just less visible, because people inside tech companies don't think of them as bureaucracy.

What surprised me at AISI was how much latitude we had, especially early on. It was set up deliberately to work more like a startup inside government. We had senior backing, a clear mandate, and real willingness to let technical people make technical decisions. So in some ways it was easier to move quickly on research priorities than in a large lab, where you're competing with many other teams and priorities for attention and resources.

The friction is real, but it sits in different places. In government it tends to be around process: hiring, contracts, security. In a big company it's more about alignment across a huge organization and its commercial priorities. Neither is free. Overall I've found the AISI version quite workable, and the people there have been very good at protecting the research team from the worst of it.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that AISI’s bureaucracy increased over time as the organization grew.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was less than people expect, and in some ways less than at DeepMind. The thing I'd say to anyone considering government work is that bureaucracy exists everywhere, it just takes different forms. At DeepMind, or any large tech company, you have a lot of process around compute allocation, around publication review, around which projects get prioritised, around coordination with the broader company. Those things are real and they take time.

At AISI, the bureaucracy was concentrated in a few specific places: hiring, procurement, and some aspects of security clearance. Hiring in particular was slower than I'd have liked at the start, because civil service hiring has rules that exist for good reasons about fairness and transparency, but they weren't designed with "we need to hire a very specific kind of ML researcher quickly" in mind. A lot of the early work was figuring out how to operate within those rules while still moving fast, and I think we did get quite good at that. We hired a lot of strong people in a short time.

But outside those areas, the day-to-day experience was quite light. The institute was set up deliberately to be unusual within government. It had a lot of autonomy, a technical leadership that understood what research needs, and strong political backing from the start, which meant we didn't have to fight for permission to do things as often as you might assume. If I wanted to start a new technical direction, I could mostly just do it. That's not so different from how it works inside a well-run research org in industry.

I think the other thing that surprised people is how much the people in government actually wanted this to work. There's a stereotype of civil servants as obstacles, and that was really not my experience. Most of the friction I hit was structural rather than people being unhelpful. So I came away thinking the main cost was speed on a few specific things, not a pervasive slowness, and that trade-off felt worth it for the kind of work we were able to do.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute any increase in bureaucracy over time to organisational growth.

astra-6.text:
It depended on which bit of bureaucracy you were dealing with. In government, there are things like hiring and procurement where you run into constraints that you wouldn’t have at DeepMind. Those can be frustrating, especially when you’re trying to move quickly.

But a large company also has bureaucracy. You have layers of management, coordination across teams, and decisions about what the organisation is trying to do. So I wouldn’t think of it as government having bureaucracy and industry not having it. The constraints show up in different places.

At AISI, having a clear mission helped a lot. There was a shared sense that this work mattered and that we needed to get on with it. That doesn’t make the administrative constraints disappear, but it makes a big difference to how much you can accomplish.

sol-6.1.text:
There are different kinds of bureaucracy. In government, you have more formal constraints around things like hiring and procurement, and those can be frustrating. But the amount of bureaucracy also depends enormously on whether people agree about what you’re trying to do. If you have a clear mission and a small team that’s aligned around it, you can move quite quickly, even within government.

So I wouldn’t describe it as simply “AISI had more bureaucracy than DeepMind.” There are things that are harder in government, but a large company has its own layers of coordination and approval. The interesting question is how much freedom the technical team has to get on with the work.
